summary: A landlocked country in south-central Africa, formerly called Northern Rhodesia, which became independent from Britain in 1964 and is known for its copper mines and Victoria Falls.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: From the 1850s the Scottish missionary Livingstone made several exploring and missionary journeys into the Zambia region, and in 1873 he died at Chitambo, in present-day Zambia, which prompted British churches to send missions. The London Missionary Society, the Church of Scotland and the Paris Evangelical Mission Society (which in 1885 preached among the Lozi in the west) successively built schools and hospitals. In 1991 President Chiluba declared Zambia a "Christian nation," which was written into the preamble of the 1996 constitution, and in recent years Pentecostal and charismatic churches have grown rapidly.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1891 missionaries of the Catholic White Fathers entered the Bemba area in the north, while the Jesuits preached in the south, and Catholic schools and hospitals spread across the country. The Catholic Church also often spoke out on human rights and governance during the one-party period and in the 1990s democratization, and is still one of the largest single denominations.

ranking.name: Others (Islam, Hinduism, Bahá'í Faith, etc.)
ranking.description: Islam arrived in the north and east in the 19th century with Arab and Swahili traders from the East African coast; during the colonial period Muslim and Hindu merchants from India also traded in towns, and Malawian migrants also brought Islam. The Bahá'í Faith arrived in the mid-20th century. The followers of these faiths together make up only a very small minority.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The preamble of Zambia's constitution declares the nation a Christian nation, religion holds an important place in social life, schools and politics, and churches are also the center of community activities. In this environment very few people state clearly that they have no religion, mainly a small number of intellectuals and young people in cities such as the capital, Lusaka.

religion.background: Zambia's peoples originally worshipped ancestors and nature spirits, and traditional chiefs also played religious roles. The explorations of missionaries such as Livingstone in the 19th century opened the spread of Christianity, and under the British South Africa Company and the Northern Rhodesia protectorate, the churches dominated schools and medical care. After independence in 1964 the first president, Kaunda, promoted the ideology of "Humanism," and in 1991 President Chiluba declared Zambia a Christian nation. Today Christianity is the mainstream and Pentecostalism continues to grow, while traditional beliefs are woven into rituals and customs.

language.official: The official language is English, with seven major indigenous languages used in education and broadcasting.

ranking.name: Bemba
ranking.description: Bemba belongs to the Bantu family and is the language of the Bemba Kingdom, which migrated in the 18th century from the Luba-Lunda region of the Congo and was originally distributed mainly in the northeast. With large-scale copper mining in the Copperbelt Province in the 1920s-1930s, Bemba miners from the north poured in, so Bemba became the common language of the Copperbelt cities and has the largest number of speakers in the country.

ranking.name: Nyanja (Chichewa)
ranking.description: Nyanja is basically the same as Chichewa of Malawi and is spoken mainly in the Eastern Province. The army and police often used this language during the colonial period, and in the process of urbanization the capital, Lusaka, also developed an "urban Nyanja" based on Nyanja, making it the common language of Lusaka and the east.

ranking.name: Tonga
ranking.description: Tonga is spoken in the Southern Province and the Zambezi Valley. When the Kariba Dam was built in 1958, more than fifty thousand Valley Tonga were forced to leave their homes, a major forced-relocation event in the history of Zambia and Zimbabwe. The Tonga are an ancient farming and herding people of the area, and their language is still widely used in the south.

ranking.name: Lozi
ranking.description: Lozi is spoken in Barotseland in the west. In the 1830s the Kololo from the south conquered the area and brought in Sotho, and the original Luyana language was gradually replaced, forming Lozi based on Sotho. The Barotse Kingdom later retained considerable autonomy under British protection, and the annual "Kuomboka" royal migration ceremony remains an important celebration today.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English was the language of administration of the British South Africa Company in the 1890s and of the Northern Rhodesia protectorate from 1924. At independence in 1964, in order to remain neutral among more than seventy ethnic groups and promote national unity, the government chose English as the sole official language, and it is widely used in schools, government and the media, though very few people speak it as a mother tongue.

language.history: Zambia has more than seventy ethnic groups, and its languages mostly belong to the Bantu family, among which Bemba, Nyanja, Tonga and Lozi are the main regional lingua francas. In the 19th century missionaries devised writing systems for many indigenous languages and translated the Bible. During the colonial period English became the language of administration and education, while urbanization in the Copperbelt mining area promoted the spread of Bemba and Nyanja. After independence English became the official language, and seven indigenous languages were designated for use in primary education and broadcasting.

ranking.name: Nshima
ranking.description: A thick maize porridge made by boiling white maize flour in water while stirring, formed into small balls and eaten by hand dipped in a relish (ndiwo) of vegetables, dried fish or meat.
ranking.history: Maize originated in the Americas and, after being brought to Africa by the Portuguese, was widely promoted during the colonial period of the 20th century to supply workers in the Copperbelt mining area, gradually replacing traditional millet, sorghum and cassava. Nshima has become the staple that Zambians must eat every day, and many feel that "if you haven't eaten nshima, you haven't eaten." Maize prices and subsidy policies have therefore remained a sensitive issue in Zambian politics.

ranking.name: Ifisashi (groundnut stew)
ranking.description: Greens such as pumpkin leaves, sweet potato leaves or rape are chopped and stewed with ground peanuts, tomatoes and onions; it tastes rich and mellow.
ranking.history: Peanuts originated in South America and were brought to Africa by the Portuguese after the 16th century, and are widely grown in northern and eastern Zambia. The Bemba stew peanut flour with various wild and cultivated vegetables, developing this nutritious side dish, whose name comes from the Bemba language. It is the most common vegetarian accompaniment to nshima and appears almost every day in rural households.

ranking.name: Chikanda (African polony)
ranking.description: The tubers of wild orchids are dried and ground into flour, cooked into a paste with peanut flour, chili and baking soda, then cooled to set; when sliced its texture is like a meat sausage, which is why it is called "African polony."
ranking.history: Chikanda is a traditional food of the Bemba of the north, once eaten in times of famine or at special festivals, and later became a popular snack in cities such as Lusaka. As demand has increased, wild orchids have been harvested in large numbers and even imported across borders from Tanzania and Malawi, leaving many terrestrial orchids in the area threatened with extinction. The dish has thus also become a focus of discussion about ecological conservation in Zambia.

ranking.name: Kapenta (dried small fish)
ranking.description: Small freshwater sardines are dried or fried and then stewed with tomatoes and onions; it is the most common protein accompaniment to nshima.
ranking.history: Kapenta originated in Lake Tanganyika, and in 1967-1968 people introduced it into the newly built Lake Kariba reservoir, where it multiplied greatly and developed into an important fishery. At night fishing boats attract schools of fish with lights and catch them, then dry them on shore and sell them. Because it is cheap and easy to keep, kapenta has become one of the most common sources of protein for urban and rural households in Zambia and Zimbabwe.

ranking.name: Mopane worms (ifinkubala)
ranking.description: Large caterpillars collected in the rainy season are gutted, boiled and dried; they can be eaten directly as a snack or stewed with tomatoes and onions, with a crisp texture and rich in protein.
ranking.history: Each year at the start of the rainy season in November-December, large numbers of moth larvae appear on the trees of the northern woodlands, and local people go up into the hills in groups to collect them, a long-standing seasonal tradition of northern peoples such as the Bemba. Dried caterpillars can be kept for months and were in the past an important source of protein in rural areas. Today dried caterpillars are also sold in city markets at no small price and regarded as a regional specialty.
